1.e4 c5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, controls d4 and e5 and prepares d4 to open the centre. Once d4 is played and the pawns are exchanged, White has an Open Sicilian: a lead in development and kingside space, against Black's central pawn majority and half-open c-file. By far the most common second move, it leads to open, extremely complex play.

1.e4 c5 2.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation
1.e4 c5 2.c3.background: Named after the Russian master Semyon Alapin (1856–1923), who championed it at the end of the 19th century. For many years it was not held in high regard, since 2...d5 was thought to give Black easy equality; it was revived in the late 1960s by Evgeny Sveshnikov and Evgeny Vasiukov, and Deep Blue played it against Kasparov in the first game of their 1996 match. Today it is considered one of the most solid and respectable Anti-Sicilians.
1.e4 c5 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4, so that ...cxd4 can be answered by cxd4 with two pawns in the centre. Black therefore has to counter in the centre at once. If White does get d4 in, an isolated d-pawn and active pieces usually result, in a quieter game than the Open Sicilian.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3.name: Closed Sicilian
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3.background: White's second most common move against 1...c5, after 2.Nf3. Many lines transpose into the Open Sicilian, the Moscow Variation or the Rossolimo Variation, and Andrew Soltis dubbed the set-up with 3.Nge2 the Chameleon System. The former world champion Boris Spassky often used the Closed Sicilian with success, even in Candidates matches.
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a knight and keeps the centre closed for now. White can still reach an Open Sicilian, build up with a kingside fianchetto, or attack on the kingside with the f-pawn. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so the direct fight for d4 is postponed, and Black can develop without trouble.

1.e4 c5 2.b3.name: Sicilian Defence: Snyder Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b3.background: Named after Robert M. Snyder, a US Chess Federation master, who published a book on the system in 1977. Nigel Short has used it occasionally, and it is a favourite of the Georgian grandmaster Tamaz Gelashvili.
1.e4 c5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, aiming down the long diagonal at d4, e5 and Black's kingside, and keeps other set-ups open. The move does nothing for the centre at once, so Black can develop freely. Sound, but it gives White less than the main second moves.

1.e4 c5 2.d3.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto, quick development and early castling, and usually leads to a closed game. The structure is solid but makes no claim on d4, so Black builds freely.

1.e4 c5 2.d4.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith–Morra Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.d4.background: The gambit proper arises after 2...cxd4 3.c3 and is named after Pierre Morra (1900–1969) of France and Ken Smith (1930–1999) of the Dallas Chess Club. Around 1950 Morra published a booklet and several articles on it, and Smith wrote a total of nine books and forty-nine articles on the gambit.
1.e4 c5 2.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: after 2...cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 White gives a pawn for quick development, open c- and d-files and pressure on f7 from a bishop on c4. Theory holds that this is not enough for the pawn, but the many traps make it a hard test for an unprepared opponent. Black can also decline the pawn and reach quieter lines.

1.e4 c5 2.f4.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack
1.e4 c5 2.f4.background: The name McDonnell Attack stems from the 14th match game between Alexander McDonnell and Louis de La Bourdonnais, played in London in 1834 and won by Black. The line is also known as the Grand Prix Attack, after the weekend tournaments held in England in the 1970s.
1.e4 c5 2.f4.strategy: Controls e5 and prepares to develop the knight and a bishop, aiming for a kingside attack. Played at once, it allows 2...d5 3.exd5 Nf6, when Black regains the pawn on d5 or gets quick development for it, which several authors regard as Black's best answer. White therefore usually develops the queen's knight first, which makes ...d5 harder, and plays f4 a move later.

1.e4 c5 2.g3.name: Sicilian Defence: Lasker–Dunne Attack
1.e4 c5 2.g3.background: The line occurred in the 1866 match between Steinitz and Anderssen, and Mark Taimanov sometimes played it.
1.e4 c5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto and keeps the centre closed, often leading to a slow, manoeuvring game. Black can strike at once with 2...d5, since 3.exd5 Qxd5 hits the rook on h1 through the gap on g2; White blocks the diagonal with a developing move and can then build up in the centre. Sound, but less ambitious than the main lines.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3.name: Sicilian Defence: Kronberger Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Na3.background: An eccentric move brought back into prominence by Vadim Zvjaginsev at the 2005 Russian Chess Championship Superfinal, where he played it three times, drawing twice and beating Alexander Khalifman.
1.e4 c5 2.Na3.strategy: Heads for a more active square and keeps c3 free for the c-pawn, away from the main lines of theory. For now the knight stands on the rim and does nothing for d4, so Black can take the centre freely. It is sound but gives White little.

1.e4 c5 2.Ne2.name: Sicilian Defence: Keres Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Ne2.background: It was a favourite of Paul Keres, whose name it carries, and it shares its ideas with the Chameleon System of 2.Nc3 and 3.Nge2.
1.e4 c5 2.Ne2.strategy: Keeps the choice open between an Open Sicilian and a closed set-up, while the f-pawn stays free to advance. For now the knight blocks the f1-bishop, and the early Ne2 is not very challenging, so Black can develop without trouble.

1.e4 c5 2.a3.name: Sicilian Defence: Mengarini Variation
1.e4 c5 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4, so that ...cxb4 can be met by axb4 and the c-pawn is deflected from the fight for d4, but it spends a tempo on the rim. After 2...Nc6 the push no longer works, since 3.b4 cxb4 4.axb4 Nxb4 simply wins a pawn, and Black develops freely.

1.e4 c5 2.a4.name: Sicilian Defence: Myers Attack, with a4
1.e4 c5 2.a4.strategy: Stops ...b5 but spends a tempo on the rim and weakens b4 for good, since the a-pawn can no longer guard it, and a black knight from c6 can use the square. Black develops freely.

1.e4 c5 2.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.b4.background: Generally considered too reckless, it is rarely seen in grandmaster play. In 1994 Joe Gallagher called it “a forgotten relic, hardly having set foot in a tournament hall since the days of Frank Marshall and Rudolph Spielmann”.
1.e4 c5 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to deflect the c-pawn and then take the centre with d4. After 2...cxb4 3.a3 d5, now considered Black's best, White has too little for the pawn and must even avoid 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.axb4, which loses the rook on a1 to 5...Qe5+.

1.e4 c5 2.c4.name: Sicilian Defence: Staunton–Cochrane Variation
1.e4 c5 2.c4.strategy: Resembles an English Opening with the king's pawn already on e4, but leaves d4 without pawn cover, since neither the c- nor the e-pawn can return to guard it. Black answers with ...Nc6 and ...e5 and gets a comfortable game, with d4 as a lasting outpost for a knight.

1.e4 c5 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4 but takes f3 from the king's knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal to the king. Black develops freely, while White's kingside pieces lack good squares.

1.e4 c5 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's pieces but spends a tempo without any gain in the centre or development. Black develops freely, and the pawn on h3 rarely proves useful.

1.e4 c5 2.h4.name: Sicilian Defence: Myers Attack, with h4
1.e4 c5 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and weakens g4 for good, since the h-pawn can no longer guard it, with nothing gained for the centre or development. Black develops freely, and the advanced pawn makes castling short less safe for White.

1.e4 c5 2.Qe2.strategy: Supports e4 but blocks the f1-bishop and brings the queen out before the minor pieces. Black develops freely, and White has nothing in the centre to show for the tempo.

1.e4 c5 2.Qf3.strategy: Takes f3 from the king's knight and exposes the queen, which ...Nc6 and ...Nd4 attack with gain of time, the knight also hitting c2, which the queen no longer guards. Black develops freely while White has to move the queen again.

1.e4 c5 2.Qg4.name: Sicilian Defence: Amazon Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Qg4.strategy: Eyes g7 and d7, but both are defended, so nothing is threatened. 2...Nf6 hits the queen and the e4-pawn at once, and the queen has to move again while Black develops with gain of time.

1.e4 c5 2.Qh5.strategy: Attacks c5 along the fifth rank and eyes f7, but brings the queen out too early. 2...Nf6 hits it: 3.Qxc5 Nxe4 regains the pawn with gain of time, and 3.Qh4 only displaces the queen, so Black gets a comfortable game.

1.e4 c5 2.Be2.strategy: Prepares Nf3 and quick castling, but the bishop is passive on e2 and no longer guards g2: after 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen hits g2, and White must spend a move blocking the diagonal.

1.e4 c5 2.Bd3.strategy: Blocks the d-pawn, and with it the c1-bishop, until the bishop on d3 moves again. Black develops freely, while White needs another bishop move to free the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Bc4.name: Sicilian Defence: Bowdler Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Bc4.background: Though once played at the highest level, for example in Anderssen–Wyvill, London 1851, it is popular today only among club players and beginners who are unfamiliar with the Sicilian.
1.e4 c5 2.Bc4.strategy: Aims at f7 and prepares quick castling, but the bishop is exposed: after 2...e6 Black follows with ...d5, opening the centre with gain of time on the bishop. The attack on f7 is easy to meet, and Black gets a comfortable game.

1.e4 c5 2.Bb5.strategy: Develops the bishop without a target, and ...a6 drives it back with loss of time; 3.Ba4 even loses it to 3...b5 4.Bb3 c4, which traps the bishop. Black gains queenside space with ...b5 as well and develops comfortably.

1.e4 c5 2.Nh3.name: Sicilian Defence: Brick Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 or g5 but sits on the rim, where it neither contests d4 nor supports e4. After ...d6 the c8-bishop eyes it, and ...Bxh3 gxh3 would wreck White's kingside pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.e5.strategy: Gains space and stops ...Nf6, but the lone pawn adds no pressure on the centre. ...Nc6 and ...d6 attack it, and White has to spend time supporting it.

1.e4 c5 2.g4.name: Sicilian Defence: Grob Variation
1.e4 c5 2.g4.strategy: Loosens the long diagonal and the squares f4 and h4 for no gain. After 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen hits the rook on h1, and after 4.Nf3 Bxg4 Black has won the g-pawn and pins the knight against the queen.

1.e4 c5 2.Ke2.name: Sicilian Defence: King David's Opening
1.e4 c5 2.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the f1-bishop and the queen's diagonal to h5. Black develops and opens the centre against a king that has nowhere safe to go.

1.e4 c5 2.Ba6.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 2...bxa6 or 2...Nxa6 wins it for nothing, because nothing defends a6.

1.e4 c5.name: Sicilian Defence
1.e4 c5.background: Giulio Cesare Polerio analysed it in a manuscript of 1594. In 1813 Jacob Henry Sarratt standardised the English name, after an old Italian manuscript that spoke of “il gioco siciliano”, the Sicilian game. Revived by Botvinnik, Boleslavsky, Bronstein and Najdorf in the 1940s and 1950s, it became, in the words of Modern Chess Openings (1990), the most played and most analysed opening at both club and master level.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6.background: Its main line, 2...Nf6 3.e5 Nd5, is the one in current practice against the Alapin and can also arise when Black declines the Smith–Morra Gambit.
1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6.strategy: Hits e4 at once while developing. White usually pushes the pawn to e5 and gains space, but the pawn then becomes a target, and Black's knight lands on an active square where it can be chased with tempo. Black aims to undermine e5 from the flank and the centre; the price is less central space for a time.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 immediately and tries to trade off White's central pawn. Black recaptures with the queen and develops quickly, but the early queen can be hit with tempo by Nc3 once White's c-pawn has been traded off, so Black has to be careful.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 e6.strategy: The most solid reply: it prepares ...d5 and steers towards French Defence structures, with White's extra c3 thrown in. The c8-bishop stays behind its pawns for now. Black gets a sound, familiar structure, but White can still aim for a slight edge.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds pressure on d4, keeping Black's central pawn moves available. It does not prevent 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4, which gives White a two-pawn centre and a slight edge. Sound enough, but a step behind the main replies.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d6.strategy: A sharp try that prepares ...Nf6 against e4. White can take the full centre at once and keep a space advantage, or accept Black's gambit by taking on c5, when Black has given up material for activity.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 g6.strategy: Heads for a kingside fianchetto, the bishop on g7 bearing on d4 from a distance. White answers 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4, and Black has to strike at the broad centre quickly, usually with 4...d5. A viable set-up, but White's extra space makes it harder than the main replies.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 e5.strategy: Stakes out d4 and makes a quick d4 awkward for White, but seriously weakens the d5 square. After 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 White has a solid edge and targets f7 and d5. Playable and rare, yet not recommended.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Qa5.strategy: Pins the c3 pawn along the e1-a5 diagonal once d2 moves, so 3.d4 cxd4 cannot be answered by 4.cxd4. White avoids the issue by developing first and playing d4 later, while the queen on a5 stands exposed. A rare try that is not refuted by force.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 b6.strategy: Prepares a queenside fianchetto with ...Bb7 to pressure e4. It is slow, though: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4 White has a broad centre and quicker development, and Nc3 easily covers e4. A rare, playable try.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Qc7.strategy: Brings the queen out early to watch e5 and the c-file, but does not stop 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4, which gives White a full centre. White's knight then gains time against the queen.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Qb6.strategy: Eyes b2 and, after exchanges on d4, the d4 pawn, but Bc1 covers b2 and 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4 builds a full centre. The exposed queen then loses time to attacks by White's knight.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Na6.strategy: The knight aims for c7 to support ...d5 but is badly placed on the rim: 3.Bxa6 bxa6 doubles Black's a-pawns at once, and 3.d4 takes the centre without a fight.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 but does nothing about d4. After 3.d4 the c1-bishop eyes h6, so Black must spend another move on the knight or accept doubled h-pawns after Bxh6 gxh6.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 in other Sicilian set-ups, but here it is slow and leaves 3.d4 unopposed, so White gets the full centre before Black has developed a piece.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space but does nothing about 3.d4, and it weakens b5, where a white bishop or knight can settle. Black spends a tempo without developing.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that prevents Bg5 but does nothing about 3.d4 and the centre, and leaves Black a tempo behind in development.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 h5.strategy: Gains kingside space but loosens g5 and g6 and does nothing about 3.d4. Black spends a tempo without developing a piece or contesting the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside for good: 3.d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against g5, so after 3...cxd4 4.cxd4 Black must spend another move holding the pawn while White has the full centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 b5.strategy: Gives up a pawn for nothing: nothing defends b5, so 3.Bxb5 wins it, and Black has no lead in development or other clear compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 c4.strategy: Overextends the pawn, which nothing defends: 3.Bxc4 takes it at once, and White then has a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 f6.strategy: Weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and takes f6 from the g8-knight: 3.Qh5+ g6 4.Qxc5 wins a pawn, and the king stays exposed.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 f5.strategy: Hangs the pawn, since 3.exf5 wins it at once, and it opens the e8-h5 diagonal against the king without any development in return.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and fights for d4 and e5 without committing a pawn. Black can wait to see which set-up White chooses, and if White drifts into an Open Sicilian, Black reaches a favourable version of it. Against a slow White set-up the game becomes a manoeuvring fight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Guards e5 and the c5-pawn and frees the c8-bishop. It keeps the main Open Sicilian set-ups available, but commits the d-pawn early and so lets White choose a different kind of game with Bb5+.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5, with a solid, flexible pawn structure. The cost is that the e6-pawn shuts in the c8-bishop for the time being. Against a slow White set-up Black can strike in the centre at once; against an Open Sicilian the game goes into a Kan or Taimanov structure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Qc7.strategy: Aims for a flexible, compact Sicilian set-up, as the queen eyes the c-file and e5. But it is committed before any piece, and Nb5 or Nd5 can hit it at once. Developing the knight first reaches the same structures without that exposure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and takes b5 from White's knight, a useful idea in many Sicilians. But it develops no piece, and White can build up without hurry.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which bears on e4 along the long diagonal. The move does little for d4 or e5 and commits Black to a slow set-up instead of a more active one.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Sets pawns on c5 and e5 against d4, as in an ordinary 1.e4 e5 game with the extra move ...c5. With both pawns advanced, neither can guard d5, so a white knight can settle there with Nd5. It gives up the usual Sicilian structure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and aims at a set-up with that bishop on the long diagonal. If White goes into an Open Sicilian, the knight on c3 keeps White from the Maróczy Bind with c4. It commits Black to the fianchetto before White has shown a plan.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it contests neither d4 nor e5 and needs another move to reach a useful square. White can also take it with Bxa6 bxa6, doubling Black's a-pawns but handing Black the bishop pair.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Qb6.strategy: Brings the queen out before any piece is developed, and it threatens nothing, because the c1-bishop guards b2. Nd5 or Na4 hits the queen at once, and White gains time while it retreats.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Qa5.strategy: Puts the queen on a5 while the pieces stay at home. It eyes c3, but the b- and d-pawns guard the knight, so the queen threatens nothing and White develops undisturbed.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Places the knight on the rim, where it eyes f5 and g4 but no central square. Once White plays d3 or d4, Bxh6 gxh6 doubles Black's pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 but runs into 3.e5, because the knight loses to Nxd5, Nxe4, Qxg4 or Qxh5 on every square except g8. Black must retreat, having spent two tempi while White gains space.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Takes b4 from White but does nothing for the centre or development. The a-pawn can no longer cover b5, so a white knight landing there cannot be driven away by ...a6.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Offers a pawn, because after 3.exd5 the queen cannot recapture: 3...Qxd5 loses it to Nxd5. Even if Black attacks the pawn with a developing move, White keeps it with natural development, and Black has little to show for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the king's knight and opens the diagonal from h5 to the king on e8. The pawn covers e5 but does nothing for development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: A rim-pawn move that does nothing for the centre or development, and gives White a free hand to build as it likes.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Advances the h-pawn without any developing or central purpose, and loosens g5 and the kingside. White continues to develop at leisure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Gives away a pawn: 3.Nxb5 or 3.Bxb5 takes it, and Black's quick development wins back a little time but not the pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Gives up a pawn: 3.exf5 takes it, and the c8-bishop cannot recapture past the d7-pawn. The opened diagonal from h5 to e8 also allows Qh5+ against Black's king.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Weakens the whole kingside and cannot hold the pawn: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 the queen attacks the rook on h8 and Bxg5 follows, with Black behind in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 c4.strategy: Gives away the pawn: 3.Bxc4 takes it at once and develops the bishop towards f7, while Black loses the c-pawn and with it all pressure on d4.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6.name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6.background: Black's most common move after 2.Nf3. It is the gateway to the Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen and Classical Variations, which arise after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...Nf6 against the e-pawn without letting White push it to e5, and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. Black builds a solid, flexible set-up and, once the c-pawn is traded for White's d-pawn, plays with a central pawn majority and the half-open c-file. The price is less space and White's lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.name: Sicilian Defence: Old Sicilian
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.background: One of Black's three main replies to 2.Nf3, with 2...d6 and 2...e6. Lines beginning 2...Nc6 that do not transpose into lines of 2...d6 have their own ECO codes, B30–B39; the most important among them are the Rossolimo, Kalashnikov, Sveshnikov and Accelerated Dragon.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece at once, controls d4 and e5 and prepares ...Nf6 without allowing e5. Black commits neither the d- nor the e-pawn and keeps the structure flexible. The cost is that White can avoid the open game with a quiet bishop move to b5 that aims at the knight and, after Bxc6, leaves Black with doubled pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6.name: Sicilian Defence: French Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6.background: One of Black's three main replies to 2.Nf3, with 2...d6 and 2...Nc6. After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 it leads to the Taimanov Variation, named after Mark Taimanov, and the Kan Variation, named after Ilya Kan and also called the Paulsen Variation after Louis Paulsen.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and prepares ...d5, building a compact pawn structure and leaving the knights and the queen to be placed later. The costs are a c8-bishop hemmed in behind the e6-pawn, a weak d6-square and a slower fight for the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.background: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, who pioneered it as one of two provocative variations of the Sicilian Defence; it is also known as the Nimzowitsch–Rubinstein Variation. After 3.e5 Nd5 it resembles Alekhine's Defence.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 at once, but White just pushes 3.e5 and the knight must move again, so White gains space and time. Black gets an unusual game built on attacking White's advanced centre, but with best play White keeps the better of it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6.background: Named after the Belgian grandmaster Albéric O'Kelly de Galway, who won the Belgian championship thirteen times between 1937 and 1959.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from White's pieces, so that after ...Nf6 and ...e5 White's knight has no jump to that square. The cost is a tempo spent on a pawn move that develops nothing, and White can sidestep the idea with a quiet pawn move.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 g6.name: Sicilian Defence: Hyper-Accelerated Dragon
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop for pressure on the long diagonal. Until the bishop arrives g7 is empty: 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 attacks the h8-rook at once, so Black must deal with that first.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qc7.name: Sicilian Defence: Quinteros Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qc7.background: Sometimes named after the Argentine grandmaster Miguel Quinteros, who introduced the move into first-class play against Henrique Mecking in 1971.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qc7.strategy: Controls e5 and keeps Black's set-up flexible, so the game often settles into a standard Sicilian set-up. The cost is an early queen move that develops no piece, and against a quiet plan with c3 and d4 the queen may be badly placed on c7.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b6.name: Sicilian Defence: Katalymov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b6.background: Named after Boris Katalymov, a Soviet and later Kazakhstani player and multiple champion of Kazakhstan. The French grandmaster Christian Bauer favours it and drew Magnus Carlsen with it in 2005.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to press on e4 along the long diagonal, but commits Black to a slower plan than the active ...b5, and Black must guard the b5-square against White's pieces. White keeps a slight plus.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qb6.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece, eyeing b2 and, once ...cxd4 has opened the diagonal, the d4-square. White develops with gain of time against the queen and keeps a lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qa5.name: Sicilian Defence: Mongoose Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qa5.strategy: Pins the d2-pawn against the king, so 3.d4 is illegal for now, but White simply blocks the diagonal and plays d4 next. The queen then does little on a5, and Black is behind in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Na6.name: Zukertort Defence: Sicilian Knight Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c7 but fights for nothing in the centre. White can ignore it and take the centre, or take it with 3.Bxa6 bxa6, which doubles Black's a-pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where e4 already controls f5, so it has little to do and the centre stays uncontested. White takes the centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the a-pawn and gives up b5 for good, since no black pawn can cover that square any more. Once White takes the centre, a white knight or bishop can settle there while Black lags in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 h6.name: Sicilian Defence: Bücker Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's pieces but spends a tempo on a pawn move that does nothing for the centre or development. White takes the centre and enjoys the freer game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and weakens g5 and the kingside, while the centre and development stay untouched. White takes the centre with d4 and develops at leisure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Supports a later ...e5, but takes f6 from the knight, weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the king, and develops nothing. White takes the centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, but White wins a tempo: 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 attacks the queen, which must retreat while White follows with d4 and a lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn: 3.Nxe5 takes it, and Black can try ...Qe7 to hit the knight and e4, but regains the pawn only at the cost of time and with a lasting weakness on d5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b5.name: Sicilian Defence: Polish Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Gives up a pawn: 3.Bxb5 takes it along the open f1-a6 diagonal, and Black's pressure on e4 or on the bishop does not offer enough compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn: 3.Nxg5 wins it, since nothing can recapture, with the c8-bishop and the queen both blocked by their own pawns. The weakened kingside offers no compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5.name: Sicilian Defence: Brussels Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Offers the f-pawn: 3.exf5 wins it, since the d7-pawn blocks the c8-bishop, and winning it back costs time. The e8-h5 diagonal to Black's king stays open for good.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 c4.strategy: Pushes the c-pawn where it cannot be defended: 3.Bxc4 wins it along the open diagonal and develops the bishop at the same time.
